presentingComplaint: Acute confusion with right-sided weakness and slurred speech for 40 minutes, found collapsed at home.
history: Type 2 diabetes for 18 years on glimepiride 4 mg twice daily and metformin, with recently added insulin glargine at night. Over the preceding two days she had reduced oral intake following a diarrhoeal illness but continued all her diabetes medication. Family found her drowsy and 'not making sense' this morning with the right arm and leg appearing weak; a stroke was suspected and she was rushed in on the acute stroke pathway. No headache, no trauma, no chest pain. She has hypertension (amlodipine, ramipril), stage 3a CKD and takes atorvastatin - polypharmacy with recent addition of a sulfonylurea dose increase by her GP. No alcohol. She was last well the previous evening. En route, ambulance capillary glucose read 'LO'.
examination: Drowsy, GCS 12 (E3 V4 M5), diaphoretic and tremulous. Pupils equal and reactive. Subtle right-sided pronator drift with reduced power (4/5) in the right arm and leg and an extensor right plantar; speech mildly dysarthric - a focal picture that raised acute stroke as the leading differential. No neck stiffness, no rash. Chest clear, abdomen soft. After a bedside glucose of 1.8 mmol/L (33 mg/dL) she was given IV dextrose, with rapid resolution of the focal deficit and return of GCS to 15 within 10 minutes - confirming Whipple's triad.

labs.cinsulin_cpeptide: endogenous pattern (high insulin, high C-peptide consistent with sulfonylurea effect)

imaging: Non-contrast CT head (stroke protocol): no acute infarct, no haemorrhage, age-appropriate involutional change - excluded intracranial catastrophe.
microbiology: Not indicated; non-infective presentation. Blood cultures not sent.
finalDiagnosis: Sulfonylurea-induced (glimepiride) hypoglycemia presenting as a stroke mimic in an elderly diabetic with CKD; neuroglycopenia with focal deficit reversed by dextrose (Whipple's triad).
citations: Endocrine Society Clinical Practice Guideline - Evaluation and Management of Adult Hypoglycemic Disorders 2023
Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine 22e - Hypoglycemia
stewardship: Non-infective diagnosis - no antimicrobials indicated. Treat with IV dextrose (25-50 mL of 25% dextrose bolus, then 10% dextrose infusion). Because glimepiride is renally cleared and the patient has CKD, anticipate protracted/recurrent hypoglycemia: admit for glucose monitoring, hold the sulfonylurea and insulin, and consider octreotide for refractory sulfonylurea-induced hypoglycemia. Avoid inappropriate empiric antibiotics for a purely metabolic encephalopathy.
contraindications: Do not restart glimepiride without dose review given CKD (eGFR 42) and low HbA1c indicating over-treatment
Avoid thiamine-free prolonged dextrose in possible malnourishment without thiamine cover
Avoid thrombolysis - hypoglycaemia is a recognised stroke mimic and glucose must be corrected/re-imaged before any lytic decision
edgeCases: Hypoglycemia can produce lateralising signs (hemiparesis, dysphasia) indistinguishable from stroke - always check glucose first on any acute neuro presentation
Recurrent hypoglycemia over 24-72h is typical with long-acting sulfonylureas plus renal impairment
Relative euglycaemia symptoms at higher glucose in long-standing tight control (low HbA1c)
expectedMaiK: Check capillary/plasma glucose immediately in any acute confusion or focal neurological deficit; hypoglycemia is a fully reversible stroke/seizure mimic, and neuroglycopenic focal signs resolve with dextrose (Whipple's triad).

Non-contrast CT head to exclude stroke/haemorrhage given focal deficit
Serial glucose monitoring (anticipate recurrence with sulfonylurea + CKD)
